@graph.headline: The Bible of Options Strategies — Summary: How to Pick the Right Strategy for Your Market View
@graph.description: Summary of Guy Cohen's The Bible of Options Strategies: use its purpose-first system and strategy table to pick the right strategy for your market view.

mainEntity.name: What is The Bible of Options Strategies?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is a strategy reference by Guy Cohen that organises options strategies by market purpose — direction, income, volatility, sideways movement, leverage, and synthetic structures — so a reader can start from what they think the market will do and find the strategies built for that view. Each strategy is explained step by step: why it works, when it is appropriate, when it is inappropriate, and how to use it.

mainEntity.name: How many strategies are in The Bible of Options Strategies?

acceptedAnswer.text: The publisher describes the book as a guide to the 60 best options trading strategies. The book itself works through 58 strategies in detail. The difference is between the publisher's catalogue count and the strategies the author actually walks through — either way, the book's value is its organisation by purpose, not the count.

mainEntity.name: Who wrote The Bible of Options Strategies?

acceptedAnswer.text: Guy Cohen, an options trader and educator and the author of the plain-English primer Options Made Easy. He is also the creator of the OVI indicator, which the second edition introduces.

mainEntity.name: Is The Bible of Options Strategies good for beginners?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not for complete beginners. Readers with no prior exposure to options fundamentals will struggle, because the book assumes you already know what a call and a put are. It is best for traders who have read a primer or a playbook and now want a reference for choosing between strategies.

mainEntity.name: Is The Bible of Options Strategies worth reading?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, for the right job. If you want one reference that answers "which strategy fits this market view?" and shows you each candidate's worst case, it is worth owning. If you want a complete trading system, a pricing theory, or depth on a single strategy, you will outgrow it — those are different books.

mainEntity.name: What is the strategy table in The Bible of Options Strategies?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is a summary table in the book's appendix that lets you look a strategy up by purpose. You state your market view, find the purpose family that matches it, and compare the candidate strategies on the same fields — what each needs to be right about, what its worst case is, and what time decay and volatility do to it. It turns the book from a catalogue into a lookup tool.

mainEntity.name: The Bible of Options Strategies vs Options as a Strategic Investment — which should I read first?

acceptedAnswer.text: Read Cohen's book first if your question is "which strategy fits my market view?" — it is organised for quick lookup and comparison. Read McMillan's Options as a Strategic Investment when you want deeper coverage of individual strategies and their mechanics. In this series' reading ladder, Cohen is the selection reference and McMillan is the depth reference.

mainEntity.name: Which edition of The Bible of Options Strategies should I buy?

acceptedAnswer.text: The second edition, published by FT Press in 2015. It is updated throughout, with new material on the current options landscape, margin collateral issues, and the OVI indicator. The first edition, from 2005, has reported errors in its worked examples, so the second edition is the one to buy.

mainEntity.name: Does The Bible of Options Strategies cover taxes?

acceptedAnswer.text: The first edition includes a chapter on taxation for stock and options traders, but it covers US tax law. Indian readers should treat it as background only — Indian tax treatment of options differs, and this book is not a guide to it.

mainEntity.name: What is the OVI indicator in The Bible of Options Strategies?

acceptedAnswer.text: The OVI is Guy Cohen's proprietary indicator, introduced in the second edition, which reads options activity to gauge market sentiment. The book summarises it in a dedicated section; it is presented as one of Cohen's tools, not as a standalone trading system, and the book does not promise results from it.

mainEntity.name: Is The Bible of Options Strategies still relevant?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, for its purpose. Strategy selection by market purpose does not go out of date, and the second edition's updates keep the framework current. What does not transfer is the book's US-specific detail — its stock-option examples and US tax chapter must be translated, not copied, by Indian readers.

mainEntity.name: Can I trade options after reading The Bible of Options Strategies?

acceptedAnswer.text: Reading it will teach you how to choose a strategy for a market view and what each strategy risks, but it will not by itself make you a profitable trader. Paper-trade the strategies first, journal every trade with its stated view and worst case, and review after twenty trades before risking real money. A strategy reference is one part of a trading education — expectancy, position sizing, and risk management are the others.
